articles.summary:

Officials said there were no reports of property damage or casualties at the time of filing the copy.
The moderate earthquake occurred at 4.30 am, with its epicentre located around 40 km northwest of Yuksom in Gyalshing district of West Sikkim, according to the National Centre for Seismology (NCS).
The NCS said the earthquake was recorded at a depth of 73 km, at latitude 27.671 degrees north and longitude 87.987 degrees east.
Mild tremors were felt in several areas of West Sikkim, as well as parts of East Sikkim, including the state capital.

articles.title: Oil below $92 amid hopes of peace talks
articles.summary: Oil prices edged lower by more than $1 on Thursday as investors increasingly hopes for peace talks to resolve the Middle East conflict as well as the much-longer lasting Russia-Ukraine war.Brent crude futures fell more than $1 to trade below $92 per barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures also lost over $1 to trade below $86 per barrel on Thursday morning. This comes after Brent crude rose over 1% on Wednesday after hitting two-month lows in the previous day.Russian and Ukrainian negotiators have agreed to a major prisoner exchange during their peace talks held over two days in Abu Dhabi, although US mediators said differences remained on other major issues, including territory. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country hoped to achieve concrete results on resolving the war this year.Also read | India's battered rupee finds an unlikely rescue party in cheaper oil and Wall Street's AI routBack in the Middle East, Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei said the government will not allow even a single particle of enriched nuclear material to leave Iran and there will be consequences if the US launches new strikes. The US meanwhile has said that nuclear issues must be part of any initial negotiations with Iran aimed at ending the eight-month-old war, while US officials downplayed the need for further military strikes.Meanwhile, OPEC+ crude oil production jumped in October, driven by a sharp increase in output from Saudi Arabia despite continued disruption to shipments through the Hormuz Strait. US crude stocks jumped by 9 million barrels in the latest week, Reuters quoted market sources as saying, citing data from the American Petroleum Institute.Where are oil prices heading for?While oil prices have dropped from their multi decade highs which they hit earlier this year, analysts remain cautious amid the seesaw political game in the Middle East. Goldman Sachs recently raised its oil price forecasts, citing increasing risks to global supplies. articles.title: Debt Mutual Funds: What investors should know before investing
articles.summary: Debt mutual funds saw a net outflow of Rs 1.8 lakh crore in September, the highest monthly withdrawal in the first half of FY27. Despite this, they remain an important investment avenue for investors looking to park surplus money, manage short-term goals and diversify their portfolios. A look at how debt funds work and what investors should know before investing.WHAT ARE DEBT MUTUAL FUNDS?Debt mutual funds invest in fixed-income instruments such as government securities, treasury bills, corporate bonds, commercial paper and certificates of deposit. They aim to provide relatively stable returns while taking lower risk than equity funds. Debt funds generate returns in two ways. The first is through the interest earned on the bonds and other securities held in the portfolio. The second comes from changes in bond prices. When bond prices rise, fund managers can book gains by selling these securities.HOW SHOULD INVESTORS CHOOSE A DEBT FUND? The choice depends on the investment horizon, liquidity needs and ability to tolerate fluctuations in returns. Investors looking to park money for a few days or months may consider overnight or liquid funds. Those with a horizon of six months to two years may look at ultra-short duration, low duration or money-market funds. For investment horizons of three years or more, categories such as short-duration funds, corporate bond funds and banking & PSU debt funds may be suitable. Gilt funds and long-duration funds are generally more appropriate for investors who understand interest-rate cycles.Read more: Smallcap mutual fund inflows drop 29% MoM to Rs 6,407 crore in October. Should investors be cautious or continue investing?WHY DID DEBT FUNDS WITNESS LARGE OUTFLOWS IN SEPTEMBER? The large outflows were largely driven by liquidity requirements rather than a change in investor appetite for debt funds. These schemes are widely used by companies and institutional investors to park surplus cash for short periods. September is also a quarter-end month when companies usually withdraw money to meet working capital requirements, advance tax payments and other financial obligations.Read more: Debt mutual funds see sharp recovery in October as quarter-end outflows reverseARE DEBT FUNDS RISK-FREE? While debt funds are generally less volatile than equity funds, they are not risk-free. One key risk is interest-rate risk. When interest rates rise, bond prices fall, which can affect the value of a fund’s portfolio. The second is credit risk, which arises when a company or other issuer fails to repay its debt or interest on time. Funds investing in lower-rated corporate bonds generally carry higher credit risk.HOW DO INTEREST RATES AFFECT DEBT FUND RETURNS? Interest rates and bond prices move in opposite directions. When interest rates fall, existing bonds offering higher interest become more attractive to investors. As demand for these bonds rises, their prices generally move up. This, in turn, tends to benefit debt funds. When interest rates rise, bond prices usually decline, which can weigh on returns. Long-duration funds are usually more affected by interest-rate changes, while liquid and overnight funds tend to see smaller fluctuations.

articles.title: Nvidia rebounds after $480 billion wipeout
articles.summary: Nvidia stock (NVDA) surged nearly 4% in premarket trading on Wednesday, November 11, as investors bought the dip after a two-day sell-off that wiped roughly $480 billion from the chipmaker's market value. Shares rose to $175.45 at 6:49 a.m. ET, up 3.88%, after closing Tuesday at $168.89, down $9.78, or 5.47%.The rebound came alongside gains in US stock futures, with Nasdaq 100 futures rising 1.67%, S&P 500 futures gaining 0.74% and Dow futures edging up 0.03%.Investors are returning to AI stocks even as Nvidia faces an investigation involving CEO Jensen Huang, just six days before its November 17 earnings report.Why is Nvidia stock rising today after a $480 billion market value crash?Nvidia's rebound comes after two difficult trading sessions. Shares fell 4.3% on Monday and another 5.47% on Tuesday as investors reacted to reports about Huang's relationship with a woman suspected by US intelligence of having links to Chinese intelligence.The stock closed Monday at $178.67 before falling to $168.89 on Tuesday. Wednesday's premarket recovery has helped Nvidia regain part of those losses, although shares remain below their level before the controversy intensified.The recovery is also part of a broader rally in AI stocks. CoreWeave shares gained more than 10% in premarket trading after its quarterly results helped ease concerns about AI infrastructure spending. Micron and Marvell also rose nearly 7%.Nvidia faces Jensen Huang investigation as board hires outside law firmNvidia confirmed on Tuesday that its independent directors had hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate whether company secrets or US national security had been compromised.The investigation will be led by former acting US Attorney Joon H. Kim.The company had already announced an independent review on Sunday. Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe that company secrets or national security had been compromised. It also expressed confidence in Huang and his leadership team.The allegations remain unproven, and China has denied claims of an espionage operation.Huang returned to Nvidia's office on Monday and continued holding meetings on Tuesday, according to CNBC. His return comes as investors assess whether the controversy could affect Nvidia's operations or leadership.Bank of America warns Nvidia could face three different outcomesBank of America outlined three possible scenarios for Nvidia in a research note on Tuesday.The first involves a contained investigation with no major disruption to leadership. Under this outcome, investor attention could return to Nvidia's earnings and AI chip demand.The second involves prolonged uncertainty that puts pressure on the company's valuation ahead of its quarterly results.The third carries greater financial risks. Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya warned that adverse findings, leadership changes or tighter restrictions could require investors to reassess Nvidia's earnings outlook.Morgan Stanley removes Nvidia stock from top picks after 25% declineMorgan Stanley removed Nvidia from its top stock picks on Wednesday after shares dropped more than 25% since the bank added the company to its list on October 2.The bank's analysts said Huang's leadership remains crucial to Nvidia's strategic direction.The decision adds to concerns about how much Nvidia's market valuation depends on its chief executive.Zacks Chief Equity Strategist John Blank also warned that investors were concerned about possible additional US restrictions and further developments in the investigation.Speaking to CNBC, Blank said the situation was negative for Nvidia, Huang and the broader AI trade.Nvidia earnings on November 17: Can NVDA stock sustain its recovery?Nvidia's next quarterly earnings report is scheduled for November 17, giving investors another major event to watch.The market will focus on revenue growth, AI chip demand, profit margins and the company's guidance for the coming quarter.

articles.summary: Tehran: Iran's army said Wednesday that an oil tanker had struck a mine and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, where the country has been targeting ships that transit without its authorisation.Since the outbreak of the Middle East war in late February, Tehran has heavily restricted traffic through the strategic waterway, insisting vessels use routes authorised by the Islamic republic.The United States has in response imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports and helped tankers travel the strait, which normally carries about one-fifth of global oil.The American military recently claimed all mines had been cleared from the strait."Early this morning, a violating oil tanker caught fire after striking a naval mine in an unsafe, prohibited area in the east of the Strait of Hormuz," the naval forces of Iran's army said in a statement carried by state TV.In recent weeks Tehran has made multiple announcements saying ships had caught fire in the strait, often claiming they struck mines.US Central Command, which oversees US military operations in the region, has been escorting ships through the waterway and said last month that it had helped Gulf countries export 1.5 billion barrels of oil via Hormuz since the summer.On Tuesday, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the ideological arm of Iran's military, said three other oil tankers had caught fire in the strait.

articles.title: Michael Burry calls Nvidia 'heck of a trade' after Huang’s scandal sparks $430 bn selloff. Why is Big Short fame dismissing fears?
articles.summary: Michael Burry is known for his bearish take on artificial intelligence-linked stocks, but the ‘Big Short’ investor dismissed worries around Nvidia following the controversy surrounding CEO Jensen Huang’s extramarital affair, calling the chipmaker a “heck of a trade”.The popular American investor sees potential for a near-term trading opportunity in Nvidia but doubts the controversy surrounding CEO Jensen Huang will damage Nvidia's business much. "Still, I believe Nvidia's competitive advantage will shrink over the next five years," he said. While Burry struck a positive note for Nvidia, he is not exactly bullish on the chipmaker. He is not tempted to make a long-term trade on the stock, but he feels the entire market will soon think it is a “heck of a trade.”Also read | Nvidia Stock Sell-Off Deepens: Spy scandal, price target cuts put AI giant under pressureAll about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair controversy Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang openly admitted that he has been in an intimate relationship with a business executive whom US intelligence reportedly alleged was a Chinese spy, leading to the company launching an investigation into the reports. This has led to a sharp selloff in Nvidia shares, wiping out around $430 billion from its market value in just two sessions.Huang, in a message to company employees released on Sunday, acknowledged having an affair and apologised to both his family and company staff. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” the 63-year-old Taiwanese-born executive said.Also read | Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang faces leadership questions as Republican senator calls for his resignationMichael Burry takes U-turn on Nvidia?Notably, Michael Burry had been shorting Nvidia shares until September, when he announced that he is exiting some of the put options. Put options typically reflect a trader’s conviction that the stock price is about to fall. Burry had long held put options on a variety of stocks which remained the face of the AI boom, spooking investors about a possible market crash when the artificial intelligence frenzy fizzles out. The American investor later exited some of the put options, triggering some optimism, but Burry clarified that it was not his intention.Burry said he sold his December 2026 puts on both Nvidia and Palantir entirely to avoid rapid time-based decay. He added that he did not replace or roll the positions, saying he is "pulling back on exposures across the portfolio." Michael Burry's AI warningsThe American investor who famously correctly predicted the 2008 US housing crisis has been sounding the alarm since the beginning of the year over a prospective big market crash when the AI frenzy fizzles out. Earlier this year, Burry said he continues to believe that the market is close to a major top, warning of a similar crash to that of 1987 when Dow Jones recorded a historic 23% plunge, which led to the introduction of regulatory circuit breakers. However, the market investor noted that the S&P 500 making new highs likely will bring new money into the market.He wrote in a Substack post that he sees many indicators, both technical and fundamental, lining up for the same conclusion as the Dotcom crash. "1999 went where no market had gone before, and I would say so can this one...It is already there on several indicators," he said, arguing that massive venture capital flows, rising AI debt issuance, and extreme market optimism are creating conditions where valuations may detach from economic reality.Also read | Anthropic retracts details of $69 billion IPO filing sent to bankers. articles.title: China builds inside Europe's walls
articles.summary: Sofia: China doesn't need to clear Europe's trade barriers. It can build inside them.Chinese companies are establishing production and supplier networks across Central and Eastern Europe, which could enable them to gain more control over the technologies and inputs that European manufacturing needs.China is increasingly challenging the European Union in the advanced manufacturing sectors that helped the EU weather the first China shock, which reshaped global manufacturing in the 2000s. Chinese firms are competing with the EU in chemicals, machinery, advanced equipment and autos - and increasingly coming out on top on both price and quality.The EU trade deficit with China has nearly quadrupled over the past decade, from around €100 billion in 2014 to over €370 billion in 2025, or roughly €1 billion a day, according to Eurostat data.France and Germany are seeking to push back with stronger trade defences, but import curbs will achieve little if Chinese investment, ownership and control of critical technologies recreates the same vulnerabilities inside the single market.LOOKING EASTCentral and Eastern Europe appear to be key to China's growth strategy in Europe.While the EU's trade deficit with China has hovered around 2% of EU gross domestic product (GDP) since 2014, it has risen sharply in parts of CEE. For example, Slovenia's goods deficit with China rose from 2.5% to 16% over that period. Meanwhile, Poland's goods deficit surged from €8.9 billion to €34.3 billion, equivalent to about 5.2% of GDP. The Czech Republic's deficit nearly quadrupled to €22 billion, or roughly 8% of GDP, and Hungary's tripled to €10.4 billion, or about 6% of GDP.Investment and corporate ties deepened that exposure. In 2025, Chinese foreign direct investment (FDI) flows into the EU approached €16.8 billion, and the cumulative value of Chinese investment in the bloc was about €95 billion, according to Eurostat and Rhodium Group data.While most legacy Chinese FDI in Europe centered on Germany, France and the Benelux countries, the focus has shifted east in recent years. CEE has attracted more than half of Chinese FDI into the EU and Britain since 2021, according to an analysis by the Rhodium Group, with an even larger regional share when the Western Balkans are included. Hungary has attracted the largest share of new investment since the COVID-19 pandemic, hitting 44% in 2023 and 23% in 2025.The investment surge in CEE has largely been driven by mega-projects in the electric vehicle (EV) supply chain. Chinese EV and battery manufacturers CATL, BYD and Sunwoda are all establishing major Hungarian operations. Slovakia has attracted investment from Chinese battery tech firm Gotion, and will be the site of a new Volvo plant owned by the Chinese automaker Geely.Meanwhile, Serbia, which has significant steel and copper assets, has signed contracts with Chinese auto firms Minth , Shanghai Automotive Chassis (SHAC), BMTS Technology and Xingyu Automotive, envisaging around €1 billion in investment and nearly 1,700 car-parts jobs, according to the government. The deals also include a new robotics factory in Sabac, billed as Europe's first humanoid robot mass production base.These investments can create jobs, spur growth, and accelerate the energy transition, but they may also erode EU competitiveness over time. Outsourcing key advanced manufacturing technologies to Chinese entities risks deepening Europe's dependence on external supply chains and weakening domestic innovation and R&D.DEFEND, THEN COMPETEEurope is seeking to limit China's access to its consumer markets and industries, but the current Franco-German push for faster defensive trade action and tougher investment screening across the bloc appears to be too little too late.Europe's flagship proposal, the Industrial Accelerator Act, leaves manufacturers' key competitiveness gaps unaddressed. Moreover, its screening mechanism would largely leave unexamined Chinese control via ultimate ownership, foreign subsidies and supply-chain concentration - some key issues when looking at CEE's growing dependence.There is also the problem of fragmentation across the bloc. Investment deals might be in one country's interest but could weaken the bloc's collective negotiating position with Beijing. To address this, the continent would likely need a permanent European economic security coordination mechanism to unite trade, competition and national screening authorities that could identify risks before investments become irreversible.Yet the chances of forming such a body at a time of growing political fragmentation within EU countries seem slim.And, ultimately, protectionism can only get Europe so far. It cannot compensate for the region's structural problems, including expensive energy, fragmented capital markets and slow industrial innovation. For that, the region would likely need to create a true energy union and invest in technological innovation. Building trade walls buys time, but not true change.(The views expressed here are those of Martin Vladimirov, director of the Geoeconomics Program of the Center for the Study of Democracy (CSD))

articles.title: HEG Advanced Materials shares gain 5% after subsidiary secures Rs 610 crore incentive under ECMS
articles.summary: Shares of HEG Advanced Materials gained 5% on Wednesday to an intraday high of Rs 305 on NSE after its subsidiary TACC received the approval letter for an incentive of Rs 609.50 crore under the Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme (ECMS) of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology.According to a filing with the exchange, the company said that the incentive is for TACC’s Synthetic Graphite Anode Material project at Sirsoda Industrial Area, Dewas, Madhya Pradesh, and is subject to scheme guidelines and prescribed conditions.The Dewas facility is spread across more than 100 acres and is planned for a committed scaled capacity of beyond 30,000 metric tonnes per annum (MTPA) by FY2028-29. The first phase of 20,000 MTPA is targeted for commissioning by June 2027.Also Read |Kalyan Jewellers shares zoom 10%, hit upper circuit after strong Q2 earnings. What analysts are saying“We are grateful to the Government of India and the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology for this support, and for their vision of building a strong electronics component manufacturing base in the country,” said Riju Jhunjhunwala, Chairman, Managing Director and CEO, HEG Advanced Materials.“The approval under ECMS is a strong endorsement of TACC’s technology and of our belief that India can build a globally competitive battery materials value chain at home. Anode material sits at the heart of every battery cell, and producing it at scale in India is central to a secure and resilient energy storage supply chain,” Jhunjhunwala further said.The company also said that the approval strengthens HEG Advanced Materials’ vision, through its wholly owned subsidiary TACC to build localized, resilient and globally competitive battery materials value chain and it is also a significant step towards strengthening India’s advanced energy storage ecosystem.“The support under ECMS strengthens our ability to execute at scale. Our Dewas facility is designed to deliver high performance synthetic graphite anode material that meets the standards of global cell manufacturers,” said Ankur Khaitan, Managing Director and CEO, TACC.Khaitan also said that, “Our focus now is on timely execution, consistent quality and close collaboration with customers to ensure supply reliability. articles.title: Hidden pain! Why did investors lose money in 750 smallcaps when Nifty rallied 2500 points?
articles.summary: The Nifty has staged a strong recovery over the past month, surging nearly 13% as foreign investors returned to Dalal Street and heavyweight stocks bounced back from their recent lows. Yet, the rally has brought little relief to hundreds of smallcap investors, with more than 750 stocks delivering negative returns during the same period.An analysis of stock market data compiled by ACE Equity shows that 769 stocks declined between October 8 and November 8, even as the benchmark Nifty recovered sharply. The Nifty climbed 2,812 points, or 12.65%, during this period.The contrasting performance highlights the narrow nature of the market recovery, with foreign institutional investors (FIIs) largely favouring established large-cap companies, while smaller stocks continue to struggle. The weakness has been particularly painful for retail investors, many of whom have substantial exposure to midcap and smallcap companies following their strong performance in previous years.Hundreds of stocks remain under pressureSeveral well-known companies feature among the stocks that have declined despite the Nifty's recovery. According to ACE Equity data, eMudhra fell 33.73% between October 8 and November 8, while Wardwizard Innovations & Mobility declined 32.53%.Genesys International lost 31.58%, Morepen Laboratories dropped 30.93%, and KRN Heat Exchanger & Refrigeration fell 30.90%. Sterlite Technologies declined 30.22%, while MTAR Technologies slipped 26.79%. Electronics Mart India lost 24.39%, Kirloskar Oil Engines fell 24.54%, and RR Kabel declined 21.44%.Other notable laggards included Netweb Technologies, down 16.91%, HFCL, down 15.88%, and Praj Industries, which lost 12.29%.Also Read: FIIs are back with a bang but why are stocks from only 2 sectors their favourites? The losses show that the market recovery has left behind a substantial number of companies across technology, pharmaceuticals, engineering, manufacturing and other sectors.For investors holding these stocks, the sharp improvement in benchmark indices has done little to offset the damage suffered during the broader market correction.Why is Nifty rising while smallcaps struggle?Apurva Sheth, Head of Market Perspectives and Research at SAMCO Securities, believes the divergence comes down to buying being concentrated in a handful of heavyweight stocks."A lot of investors are scratching their heads thinking why their portfolio isn't moving up with Nifty. The simple answer is you don't own what is moving up," Sheth said.According to his analysis, the Nifty Top 10 Equal Weight Index gained 10.64% over the preceding month, while the Nifty Midcap 150 and Nifty Smallcap 250 indices each declined 2.74%. The Nifty Microcap 250 fell 5.32%.The first major reason behind the divergence is valuation. Several largecap stocks had suffered heavy losses during the market correction that began in January 2026, bringing their valuations to more attractive levels.This encouraged investors to return to established companies as crude oil prices eased and concerns about the global economic outlook moderated.Smaller companies, meanwhile, entered the correction with relatively elevated valuations following their earlier rallies. Investors have remained selective amid concerns about earnings visibility and the sustainability of growth.Foreign money is chasing large companiesThe second major factor is the return of foreign institutional investors. After months of sustained selling, overseas investors have begun deploying substantial capital into Indian equities, helping lift banking, technology, telecommunications and other heavyweight stocks.Foreign investors have bought more than $4.1 billion worth of Indian equities so far in November, according to Reuters, marking the strongest monthly inflow since September 2024. However, foreign institutions generally prefer large, liquid companies where they can deploy substantial amounts without significantly affecting share prices.This has benefited stocks such as ICICI Bank, HDFC Bank, Infosys, Bharti Airtel and Reliance Industries. According to Sheth, ICICI Bank and Infosys each gained 16% over his one-month review period, while Bharti Airtel advanced 14.61%. Kotak Mahindra Bank rose 10.08%, HDFC Bank gained 10%, and Reliance Industries climbed 8.44%.The ten heavyweight stocks in his analysis delivered an average return of 10.19%, highlighting how concentrated the rebound has been.For smaller companies, the absence of similar institutional buying has limited the recovery despite improving sentiment across the broader market.Can the broader market catch up?The broader market has also faced pressure from stretched valuations, uneven earnings performance and reduced risk appetite following months of geopolitical uncertainty and high crude oil prices.Although the September-quarter earnings season has shown signs of improvement, investors are increasingly distinguishing between companies delivering sustainable profit growth and those whose earlier valuations were driven by aggressive expectations.The next test for Dalal Street will be whether sustained foreign inflows and stronger corporate earnings encourage buying beyond the largest companies.Disclosure: This article was written by Podishetti Akash, who is not a SEBI-registered Research Analyst or an Investment Adviser. Iran crisis fuels a crude war in Myanmar
articles.summary: Myaing, Myanmar: Myanmar's small-scale oil prospectors are under fire from all sides as rebels and the military battle to capture a cottage industry increasingly lucrative amidst the Middle East energy shock."As long as we work here, bad luck can kill us," said Htun Aung, a worker on an artisanal oil well in Myanmar's arid heartlands.Also read | Jensen Huang case: Nvidia CEO love affair scandal revives push for tougher US line on China"But if the reality of death is hard to face, then making a living is even harder," said the 52-year-old, speaking under a pseudonym for security reasons.Myanmar imports 90 percent of its fuel oil, official figures show, making it particularly vulnerable to supply issues caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran.But the central region of Magway hosts a hardscrabble industry of domestic prospectors manning grimy derricks that squelch up crude oil in humble quantities.The area is dubbed "Anyar Dubai", associating the Anyar landscape with the oil boom Emirate, despite the pitiable $50 per week earned by workers like Htun Aung who spend their days drenched in foul crude run-off.With prices at Myanmar's petrol pumps nearly double what they were in late February, the underground "black gold" is an increasingly coveted prize of war.Also read | Trump's Iran war may be 'militarily' over, but economic siege still haunts"We just want to live in peace," said Htun Aung. "But now they strike from one side and the others strike from the other -- they keep attacking each other.""We've had to flee three, four, five times already," he added. "We run here, we run there. We fill up our motorbikes with fuel and run again."Digging inAllied pro-democracy rebels claim to have controlled oil fields in Magway's Myaing township since 2023, the third year of a nationwide civil war triggered by a coup.They patrol the dusty territory in a westward crook of the Irrawaddy river in ragtag columns and outfitted with rocket-propelled grenades, flak jackets, tote bags and flip-flops.Air and drone strikes in Myaing so far this year have already exceeded 2025's total, according to ACLED, a monitor that estimates more than 100,000 people have died since the putsch.Rebels shelter in foxholes, camouflaged among thousands of oil wells dug in an unregulated practice dating back centuries.Engine winches chug day and night, plunging plumbing tubes dozens of metres down boreholes before dragging them up filled with crude oil slurry.Prospectors pay landowners up to $3,500 to lease a spot to drill,one veteran said, with no guarantee they will hit oil.Some wells yield dribbles while others gush profit, filling tarpaulin-lined pits and barrels with oil hauled off to improvised refineries for processing into petrol and diesel."Anyar Dubai" has been "going viral" for its plentiful supply, said rebel spokesman Pyae Phyo Kyaw, at a time when Myanmar military-held areas have been rationing petrol.He touted recent offensives fending off military advances, but admitted being battered by counter-attacks."We see it primarily as an attempt to destroy what has been a strong supply route and source of revenue for us," said the 35-year-old, speaking under his real name.Myanmar's military could not be reached for comment.But in September, a month-long military operation claimed to have captured over 130 wells in Myaing and 735 more in neighbouring Pakokku township.Black marketScores of pro-democracy factions and ethnic minority armed groups are fighting the military over the 2021 coup that ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi.As the war grinds on, all sides battle to fill war chests with the tax or trade of natural resources: gem mines, rare earth mineral deposits, gold or teak.Oil projects are not generally contested.The major ones are under staunch military guard, and on-the-books output is tiny by international standards -- around 6,000 barrels a day last year, according to the US Energy Information Administration.But artisanal fields are coveted by rebels precisely because of their modest size, according to Thomas Kean, senior Myanmar consultant for the International Crisis Group."Part of the reason why they're significant is because they're not globally significant," he said, explaining that they are small enough to thrive under the radar, yet big enough to fund guerrillas.Spiking oil prices may not directly drive conflict, said Kean, highlighting a broader military campaign to evict rebels from heartland footholds by squeezing revenue sources.But as the spoils of war become more profitable, the stakes get higher."We're talking about millions of barrels a year coming out of these oil fields," he added."With global prices what they are, that's a significant amount of money."
